lesson.title: Rational and irrational numbers
points: A rational number can be written as p/q with q not equal to 0. Its decimal either stops (0.25) or repeats forever (0.333...).
An irrational number has a decimal that never stops and never repeats a block, like √2 and π. The fraction 22/7 is only an approximation of π.
Rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers, and every real number has a place on the number line.
Laws of exponents: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) and (a^m)^n = a^(mn). To rationalise 1/(√a + √b), multiply top and bottom by (√a − √b).
lesson.story: Share one roti equally among 3 friends: each gets 0.333... of a roti, a decimal that repeats forever but is still the fraction 1/3. But the diagonal of a 1 m square tile is √2 m, and its decimal never settles into any pattern.

lesson.title: Polynomials and their zeros
points: A polynomial in x has only whole-number powers of x, like 3x² − 5x + 2. Its degree is the highest power.
A zero of p(x) is a number a for which p(a) = 0.
Remainder theorem: when p(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is p(a). Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(a) = 0.
Useful identities: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y², (x − y)² = x² − 2xy + y², and x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y).
lesson.story: When you check whether 12 divides 60, you look at the remainder. Remainder 0 means 12 is a factor. The factor theorem does the same for polynomials: if p(a) = 0, then (x − a) divides p(x) exactly.

example.q: Find the remainder when p(x) = x³ + 2x² − x + 5 is divided by (x − 1).

lesson.title: Locating points on a plane
points: Two number lines cross at right angles: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis. They meet at the origin (0, 0).
A point is written (x, y). The x-value (abscissa) comes first and tells how far left or right; the y-value (ordinate) tells how far up or down.
The axes divide the plane into four quadrants. Quadrant I is (+, +), II is (−, +), III is (−, −) and IV is (+, −).
A point on the x-axis looks like (a, 0) and a point on the y-axis looks like (0, b).
lesson.story: In a cinema hall your ticket says row 5, seat 8. You walk to the row first and then to the seat. A point (x, y) works the same way: the order matters, so (5, 8) and (8, 5) are different places.

lesson.title: Equations with two unknowns
points: A linear equation in two variables looks like ax + by + c = 0, where a and b are not both zero.
A solution is a pair (x, y) that makes the equation true. Such an equation has infinitely many solutions.

lesson.title: Congruent triangles and inequalities
points: Two triangles are congruent when they match exactly in all sides and angles. The valid rules are SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS.
Equal angles alone (AAA) or two sides with a non-included angle (SSA) do not prove congruence.
In a triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal, and the larger side lies opposite the larger angle.
The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.

lesson.title: Area and volume of solids
points: Cuboid: total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl) and volume = lbh. Cube: total surface area = 6a² and volume = a³.
Cylinder: curved surface area = 2πrh, total surface area = 2πr(r + h) and volume = πr²h.
Cone: slant height l = √(r² + h²), curved surface area = πrl and volume = (1/3)πr²h.
Sphere: surface area = 4πr² and volume = (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: curved area = 2πr², total area = 3πr² and volume = (2/3)πr³.

lesson.title: Mean, median, mode and chance
points: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values. Median is the middle value after arranging in order; for an even count, average the two middle values. Mode is the value that occurs most often.
In a histogram the bars touch each other because the class intervals are continuous.
Empirical probability = number of times the event happened ÷ total number of trials.
A probability is always between 0 and 1, including both.
